title: Density-Aware Reward Scaling: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Reward-Proportional Sampling

paper.title: Density-Aware Reward Scaling: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Reward-Proportional Sampling
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement learning objectives that maximize expected return can concentrate probability mass on a small subset of high-reward outcomes, limiting diversity when multiple distinct solutions are desirable.
We introduce Density-Aware Reward Scaling (DARS), a simple reward-processing mechanism that promotes reward-proportional sampling in continuous outcome spaces while retaining standard policy-gradient training.
DARS estimates the local density of outcomes within each on-policy rollout group and inversely scales rewards by this density.
The method requires no learned density model, auxiliary objective, critic, or modification to the underlying policy-gradient objective.
In a controlled multimodal navigation task, DARS-GRPO avoids the single-mode collapse exhibited by GRPO and closely recovers the target mode allocation.
Applied to text-to-image prompt adaptation, DARS-GRPO consistently improves image and prompt diversity across datasets, Policy LMs, and reward settings while maintaining good semantic alignment.
These results show that density-aware reward scaling provides a lightweight way to improve coverage of diverse high-reward outcomes within existing reinforcement-learning pipelines.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning is typically formulated to maximize expected return, which can drive outcome-level probability mass toward a small subset of high-reward outcomes ( GX-Chen et al. 2025 ) . While desirable for conventional control problems, this behavior is limiting in domains where multiple distinct outcomes are simultaneously valuable. In generative modeling, scientific discovery, and structured prediction, the objective is often not merely to identify a high-reward solution, but to learn a policy that maintains broad coverage over the high-reward outcome space. Several approaches have been proposed to promote such diversity. Entropy-regularized RL encourages stochastic action selection, but action-level stochasticity does not in general specify a desired distribution over terminal outcomes ( Haarnoja et al. 2018 ) . Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) instead target reward-proportional sampling, providing a principled framework for generating diverse high-reward samples ( Bengio et al. 2023 ) . Applying GFlowNet-style objectives to autoregressive pretrained models generally requires formulating generation through flow- or trajectory-based objectives rather than retaining an unchanged policy-gradient training pipeline ( Yun et al. 2025 ) . Inverse Probability Scaling (IPS) offers another route by inversely scaling reward according to terminal-outcome visitation probability ( Sinha et al. 2026 ) . In continuous or high-dimensional outcome spaces, however, exact repeated outcomes may be rare or may not provide a meaningful notion of semantic equivalence. We introduce Density-Aware Reward Scaling (DARS), a simple framework for encouraging a policy that has reward-proportional behavior within standard policy-gradient reinforcement learning. DARS is motivated by the limitations of IPS and replaces discrete visitation frequency with an estimate of local outcome density in continuous outcome spaces. For each on-policy rollout group, outcomes that lie in densely populated regions receive proportionally reduced rewards, while high-reward outcomes in underrepresented regions receive greater relative rewards. This density scaling is applied before advantage estimation and requires no modification to the underlying policy-gradient objective. Importantly, DARS introduces no learned density model, critic, auxiliary loss, or specialized policy architecture; instead it simply modifies reward processing within the existing RL pipeline. Our central contribution is a simple mechanism for mitigating outcome collapse and promoting coverage of diverse, high-reward regions within standard policy-gradient training. We validate DARS through controlled synthetic experiments that establish its ability to approximate reward-proportional sampling, followed by text-to-image prompt adaptation experiments demonstrating improved diversity while preserving generation quality, and kernel-width ablations that provide mechanistic evidence for its density-aware reward scaling.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Mode collapse in RL and loss of diversity: Mode collapse is widely associated with generative models that represent only a small subset of a multimodal data distribution. An analogous failure occurs in reinforcement learning at the level of terminal outcomes: even when multiple trajectories or solutions receive similar rewards, expected-return optimization concentrates the learned policy on a narrow subset of them, reducing the diversity of generated solutions in language and image generation ( Kirk et al. 2024 ; Chen et al. 2026 ) . Existing approaches mitigate this behavior through entropy regularization, KL constraints, reward shaping, or diversity-aware objectives ( Schulman et al. 2017 ; Liu et al. 2026 ) , yet they do not directly control the distribution of terminal outcomes. Recent work instead attributes outcome collapse to expected-return optimization itself, where an outcome’s aggregate learning signal is amplified by its current sampling probability, creating a rich-get-richer feedback loop ( Sinha et al. 2026 ) . Reward-proportional methods address this issue by sampling outcomes in proportion to their rewards: GFlowNets achieve this through specialized flow-conservation objectives and have been extended to multi-objective optimization, continuous state spaces, prompt adaptation, and language-model reasoning ( Bengio et al. 2021 ; Bengio et al. 2023 ; Jain et al. 2023 ; Lahlou et al. 2023 ; Zhu et al. 2026 ) , while IPS instead rescales rewards using inverse visitation probabilities estimated from empirical outcome frequencies ( Sinha et al. 2026 ) . However, empirical visitation frequencies become ineffective in continuous outcome spaces, where exact outcome repetitions are exceedingly rare. Concurrent work ( Chen et al. 2026 ) , also adjusts GRPO rewards using within-group semantic redundancy for mathematical reasoning in LLMs. In contrast, we study density-aware reward scaling as a mechanism for reward-proportional sampling in continuous outcome spaces and directly evaluate recovery of the target reward distribution. Prompt Adaptation and Image Generation: Loss of output diversity has become increasingly visible in reinforcement learning from human feedback and other forms of large-language-model post-training ( Ouyang et al. 2022 ; Kirk et al. 2024 ; Chen et al. 2026 ) . Reward optimization can favor a narrow set of response styles or semantic patterns even when many responses are valid. In practice, this behavior is often moderated with KL regularization, reward mixing, early stopping, or stochastic decoding. Prompt-optimization methods learn rewrites that improve text-to-image quality or alignment ( Hao et al. 2023 ) , while PAG learns diverse effective prompts with a GFlowNet formulation over prompt-generation trajectories ( Yun et al. 2025 ) . CADS acts at diffusion inference time by annealing the conditioning signal during sampling.

sections.heading: 3 Density-Aware Reward Scaling (DARS)
sections.text: IPS shows that reward-proportional sampling can be achieved by inversely scaling rewards according to outcome probabilities under the current policy ( Sinha et al. 2026 ) , but estimating these probabilities through exact visitation frequencies does not extend naturally to continuous outcome spaces, where repeated outcomes are unlikely. DARS instead represents outcomes in a continuous feature space where distances capture meaningful similarity between outcomes. This representation allows visitation to be defined over local regions rather than exact outcome identities. DARS estimates the local density of each sampled outcome within its on-policy rollout group and inversely scales its reward by this density, reducing reinforcement of densely sampled regions while relatively favoring underrepresented high-reward regions.

sections.heading: 3.2 Integration with GRPO
sections.text: DARS modifies only the reward-processing stage of the GRPO pipeline. GRPO uses a clipped policy-ratio objective, and estimates advantages from groups of sampled outputs ( Shao et al. 2024 ) . It replaces each task reward R i R_{i} with the density-scaled reward R ~ i \widetilde{R}_{i} from Equation ( 3 ), after which the group-relative advantage is computed as A i = R ~ i − R ~ ¯ s R ~ , A_{i}=\frac{\widetilde{R}_{i}-\overline{\widetilde{R}}}{s_{\widetilde{R}}}, (4) where R ~ ¯ \overline{\widetilde{R}} and s R ~ s_{\widetilde{R}} are the within-group mean and standard deviation of the scaled rewards. The resulting advantages are passed to the standard GRPO objective without further modification. For each conditioning input, DARS-GRPO samples an on-policy rollout group and evaluates its task rewards. It then computes the within-group local-density scores, scales and normalizes the rewards to obtain group-relative advantages, and applies the standard GRPO policy update without further modification. Thus, DARS requires no change to the GRPO policy ratio, clipped surrogate objective, policy architecture, or optimization procedure; its sole intervention is density-aware reward scaling before advantage normalization.

sections.text: At either kernel width extremes, as h → 0 h\to 0 , ρ i ≈ 1 \rho_{i}\approx 1 and the rewards remain unchanged; as h → ∞ h\to\infty , ρ i ≈ G \rho_{i}\approx G and group-relative advantage normalization cancels the shared reward scale. Intermediate bandwidths instead produce non-uniform reward scaling across the given rollout group, thereby modifying the resulting policy-gradient signal. The primary comparison is against GRPO: both methods use the same policy, environment, and terminal reward, but only DARS corrects for local outcome collapse. GFlowNet provides a reward-proportional reference with a different training objective. The experiment is a controlled empirical test of whether DARS approaches the normalized reward distribution. sections.heading: 4.1 Baselines and Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: We compare GRPO and DARS-GRPO, using GFlowNet as a non-RL reward-proportional reference. We evaluate the terminal distribution produced by each trained policy using 10 6 10^{6} sampled terminal states per trained policy. Target samples are drawn from the Gaussian mixture and rejected when they fall outside the unit square. We use complementary metrics because no single score captures all forms of distributional mismatch in a multimodal setting. Mean raw reward is estimated as the empirical average of r ⁡ ( x ) r(x) over sampled terminal states. Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) and histogram total variation (Hist. TV) compare the empirical and target densities on a 100 × 100 100\times 100 grid. Sliced Wasserstein-2 ( SW 2 \mathrm{SW}_{2} ) ( Kolouri et al. 2019 ) , energy distance ( Székely et al. 2013 ) , and Sinkhorn divergence ( Feydy et al. 2019 ) compare generated and target samples directly and measure geometric mismatch. RBF maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) ( Gretton et al. 2012 ) is reported at several bandwidths: small bandwidths emphasize local component shape, whereas large bandwidths emphasize mode allocation and global structure. Sliced Wasserstein-2 and energy distance use ten repetitions of 20,000 20{,}000 samples, while Sinkhorn divergence uses 500 500 samples. For mode-level evaluation, each terminal state is assigned to its nearest target center. From these assignments, we compute the mass of each mode, the minimum mode mass, and mode TV which measures deviation from uniform target mode weights. Precision is the fraction of generated samples lying inside k k -nearest-neighbor neighborhoods of target samples, while recall is the fraction of target samples covered by neighborhoods induced by generated samples ( Kynkäänniemi et al. 2019 ) . Precision therefore measures off-target generation, whereas recall diagnoses missing support and mode collapse. We measure Wasserstein error at two scales: the between-mode term evaluates mode weights and centers, while the within-mode term evaluates each mode’s mean and covariance. Their sum defines the hierarchical score, W hier = W between + W within . W_{\mathrm{hier}}=W_{\mathrm{between}}+W_{\mathrm{within}}. HDR outside mass is the fraction of generated samples outside the target’s 95% highest-density region. Since the target assigns approximately 0.05 probability mass outside this region, we report the calibration error | m outside − 0.05 | |m_{\mathrm{outside}}-0.05| , for which lower values indicate better agreement with the target.

sections.heading: 4.2 Results and Interpretation
sections.text: The primary result is the comparison with GRPO. In the reported run, GRPO concentrates on a single high-reward mode, whereas DARS-GRPO assigns substantial mass to all four modes and approaches their target weights. The DARS-GRPO point estimates are closer to the target than GRPO across the metrics reported in Table 1 . GRPO’s higher mean raw reward reflects tight concentration near one of four equally high peaks, rather than agreement with the normalized reward distribution. Thus, within this controlled environment, the reported run provides evidence that density reweighting prevents the evaluated policy from concentrating on one mode, recovers the correct mode weights, and improves global geometric agreement with the known target relative to GRPO. This is the central controlled contribution of the experiment. DARS-GRPO closely matches, and on several key metrics surpasses, GFlowNet despite requiring only a simple reward-scaling modification within a standard policy-gradient pipeline. Both methods achieve identical precision, indicating equally accurate recovery of high-reward outcomes. DARS consistently improves metrics that capture the global reward distribution, including sliced Wasserstein, energy distance, mode total variation, minimum mode mass, hierarchical Wasserstein error, HDR outside mass, and most larger-bandwidth MMD and Sinkhorn metrics, demonstrating more faithful recovery of target mode proportions and global geometry. GFlowNet performs slightly better on metrics emphasizing fine-scale local density, such as Jensen–Shannon divergence, histogram total variation, within-mode Wasserstein error, recall, and small-bandwidth MMD, reflecting its specialized flow-based objective. Nevertheless, these results show that a lightweight modification to conventional policy-gradient RL is sufficient to achieve reward-proportional behavior that is competitive with a substantially more sophisticated algorithmic framework. Having established in a controlled setting that DARS approximates reward-proportional sampling, we next ask whether this property is useful in a real continuous-output RL problem where the target reward distribution is unknown.

sections.heading: 5 Text-to-Image Prompt Adaptation
sections.text: Figure 2: Overview of DARS-GRPO for text-to-image prompt adaptation. A trainable language-model policy samples G G rewrites of an input prompt, and a frozen text-to-image model generates one image per rewrite. Each image receives a task reward r i r_{i} and is mapped by a frozen image encoder into a representation space, where a Gaussian kernel computes its within-group density ρ i \rho_{i} . DARS forms the scaled reward r ~ i = r i / ρ i \tilde{r}_{i}=r_{i}/\rho_{i} , reducing the contribution of high-reward images in dense representation-space regions and increasing the relative contribution of high-reward images in sparsely represented regions. GRPO then uses these scaled rewards to update only the prompt-rewriting policy.

sections.heading: 5.1 Motivation
sections.text: Prompt adaptation for image generation refers to the setting in which a language model rewrites the input prompt to match a desired set of outcomes before image generation. Text-to-image prompt adaptation provides a natural real-world benchmark for evaluating reward-proportional reinforcement learning. Unlike the synthetic experiments in Section 4 , where the target reward distribution is explicitly known, the reward-proportional distribution over generated images is intractable and cannot be directly characterized. A single text prompt typically admits many semantically faithful realizations that differ in composition, viewpoint, lighting, object arrangement, or artistic style while remaining equally valid. Since the underlying reward distribution is unavailable, directly measuring reward-proportional sampling is infeasible. Instead, we evaluate its consequences through observable proxies. If DARS successfully distributes probability mass across multiple high-reward regions, it should produce a more diverse set of images while preserving prompt alignment and image quality. We therefore measure visual diversity together with alignment and preference metrics as an indirect estimate of improved coverage of the latent reward landscape. Consequently, the objective is not merely to identify a single high-reward image, but to maintain coverage over the diverse set of high-quality outcomes consistent with the prompt. Since input prompts are the conditioning signal in diffusion models, semantically faithful prompt rewrites help steer the generation in desired directions. Learning a distribution over such rewrites therefore provides an effective mechanism for exploring multiple high-reward image modes while keeping the underlying image generator fixed. Following this formulation, we fine-tune a language model using reinforcement learning to rewrite input prompts. Images generated from the rewritten prompts are rewarded as defined in section 5.2 . Since multiple visually distinct images can achieve comparable rewards, broader coverage of the latent reward landscape should translate to greater image diversity without sacrificing fidelity. To quantify this diversity, we measure distances in the DINOv2 representation space as a proxy for perceptual similarity ( Oquab et al. 2023 ) . GRPO produces nearly identical rewrites and visually similar nighttime scenes, whereas PAG introduces moderate variation and DARS-GRPO generates more diverse rewrites, settings, and visual compositions.

Fidelity alone does not ensure that an image is aesthetically strong, whereas optimizing aesthetics alone can favor attractive images that drift from the requested content. We measure semantic alignment using the image-text cosine similarity from a CLIP model ( Radford et al. 2021 ) . A binary semantic gate determines whether the image is sufficiently aligned with the original prompt. sections.heading: 5.3 Density Calculation and Reward Scaling
sections.text: DARS estimates local density in the space of generated images, since our objective is to promote diversity over visual outcomes rather than textual rewrites. As discussed in Section 3.1 , we instantiate ϕ \phi using a frozen DINOv2 encoder, which maps each generated image i i to its unnormalized class-token (CLS) embedding y i y_{i} . Local densities are then estimated in this representation space. For a group of G G images, let y i ∈ ℝ 768 y_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{768} denote the feature vector of image i i . We compute the local density score for image i i using a Gaussian kernel as ρ i = ∑ j = 1 G K h ​ ( y i , y j ) = ∑ j = 1 G exp ⁡ ( − ∥ y i − y j ∥ 2 2 2 ​ h 2 ) . \rho_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{G}K_{h}(y_{i},y_{j})=\sum_{j=1}^{G}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert y_{i}-y_{j}\rVert_{2}^{2}}{2h^{2}}\right). (9) Following Equation ( 3 ), DARS rescales the task reward as R ~ i = R i / ρ i \widetilde{R}_{i}=R_{i}/\rho_{i} . We use this scaled reward to optimize the prompt-rewriting policy with DARS-GRPO.

sections.heading: 5.4 Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: We evaluate each prompt-rewriting policy along three complementary dimensions: image diversity, rewrite diversity, and image fidelity or preference. Image diversity is measured in DINOv2 CLS representation space using the Vendi Score ( Friedman and Dieng 2023 ) of the cosine-similarity matrix of L2-normalized CLS embeddings, and the mean pairwise Euclidean distance between CLS embeddings. Rewrite diversity is measured analogously in CLIP text-embedding space using Prompt Vendi and the mean pairwise cosine distance among rewritten prompts. Finally, CLIP-align, HPSv2 ( Wu et al. 2023 ) , and PickScore ( Kirstain et al. 2023 ) assess the semantic compatibility and human-preference-style quality of each generated image relative to the input prompt. CLIP-align is the nonnegative cosine similarity between the L2-normalized CLIP embeddings of a generated image and its original prompt. Diversity metrics are computed within each group of rewrites or images generated for the same original prompt and then averaged across the evaluation set, following within-prompt conditional evaluation. For all metrics, higher values indicate greater diversity or stronger fidelity and preference, respectively.

sections.heading: 5.5 Experiment Details
sections.text: We use a frozen Stable Diffusion v1.4 generator ( Rombach et al. 2022 ) and optimize only the prompt-rewriting policy. For all baselines and reward functions, both Qwen3-0.6B(base) ( Yang et al. 2025 ) and GPT-2 (124M) ( Radford et al. 2019 ) are already supervised fine-tuned on a shared set of curated prompt rewrites. We then train the models on 1,024 randomly sampled MS-COCO prompts ( Lin et al. 2014 ) and evaluate them on disjoint MS-COCO and Lexica prompts ( Shen et al. 2023 ) . DARS uses h = 20 h=20 for Gaussian kernels, and the alignment reward uses a CLIP-similarity threshold of 0.2 0.2 . We compare DARS-GRPO with vanilla GRPO, PAG, and GFlowNet prompt optimization, together with Stable Diffusion v1.4 with random seed initialization and CADS ( Sadat et al. 2024 ) as control baselines. All methods are evaluated using the same held-out prompts, generation budget, diffusion model, and sampling procedure. Diffusion seeds are sampled independently across methods, so image-diversity metrics also capture variation introduced by stochastic diffusion sampling while prompt-diversity metrics are unaffected by this confound.

Further, among all prompt-adaptation methods, it achieves the highest DINO pairwise distances and Image Vendi scores, indicating that density-aware reward scaling broadens the learned rewrite distribution and increases coverage in DINOv2 image-representation space. The high Prompt Vendi and diversity scores further indicate that this image diversity arises from diverse prompt rewrites, while CLIP-align, HPSv2, and PickScore imply close image fidelity. Changing the reward function affects performance across all metrics, showing that DARS responds to the reward landscape rather than producing diversity gains randomly. Having demonstrated the effectiveness of DARS on a real-world RL problem with an intractable reward-proportional distribution, we next study the effect of the kernel width used for local density estimation on the learned outcome distribution.

For the experiments in Section 5 , we demonstrate the direct effects of varying kernel widths on image-diversity produced by DARS (Table 3 ). Diversity metrics consistently peak at intermediate kernel widths and degrade when the bandwidth is either too small or too large, while image quality remains largely unchanged. This behavior reflects how DARS estimates local outcome density. With a very small kernel width, nearly every generated image appears isolated, causing density estimates to be dominated by self-similarity and resulting in almost uniform reward scaling. Conversely, an excessively large kernel width treats distant images as belonging to the same neighborhood, oversmoothing density estimates and diminishing the relative reward differences that encourage exploration. Intermediate kernel widths instead resolve meaningful local neighborhoods allowing for effective density estimation in DARS.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations
sections.text: DARS relies on a meaningful representation space and kernel bandwidth for estimating local outcome density. Its effectiveness may therefore degrade when embedding distances poorly reflect semantic similarity or when no single bandwidth captures the relevant neighborhood structure. The pairwise density computation also scales quadratically with rollout-group size, potentially limiting its use with large groups. Our experiments focus on a controlled navigation task and text-to-image prompt adaptation with fixed image representations and generators. Broader evaluation across RL domains, policy architectures, and learned representations is needed. Finally, our results establish empirical approximation to reward-proportional sampling rather than a general convergence guarantee.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced Density-Aware Reward Scaling (DARS), a lightweight mechanism for promoting diverse, high-reward outcomes within standard policy-gradient training. By inversely scaling rewards using local outcome density, DARS counteracts repeated reinforcement of densely sampled regions without requiring a critic, auxiliary objective, learned density model, or modified policy-gradient loss. In a controlled multimodal navigation task, DARS-GRPO prevents the mode collapse observed with GRPO and closely recovers target mode allocation. In text-to-image prompt adaptation, it consistently increases prompt and image diversity across datasets, Policy LMs, and reward settings while retaining semantic fidelity. These results position density-aware reward scaling as a simple yet effective approach to improving outcome coverage.

sections.heading: Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: Evaluation follows the same protocol for all methods. For each evaluation prompt, the policy generates N = 64 N=64 rewritten prompts, each of which is used to generate one image under identical diffusion sampling settings. Diversity metrics are computed only among images originating from the same source prompt and are then averaged across the evaluation set. Image-text alignment is measured using OpenAI CLIP ViT-L/14, while image diversity is computed from DINOv2 image embeddings. The aesthetic LAION predictor ( sac+logos+ava1-l14-linearMSE ) is used wherever aesthetic reward is required. During training, model checkpoints are periodically evaluated on the validation set using the same evaluation protocol. The checkpoint used for all reported experiments is selected based on the highest validation Vendi Score after reward saturation, ensuring that model selection aligns with the diversity objective optimized by DARS.

We introduce Density-Aware Reward Scaling (DARS), a simple reward-processing mechanism that promotes reward-proportional sampling in continuous outcome spaces while retaining standard policy-gradient training. DARS estimates the local density of outcomes within each on-policy rollout group and inversely scales rewards by this density. The method requires no learned density model, auxiliary objective, critic, or modification to the underlying policy-gradient objective. In a controlled multimodal navigation task, DARS-GRPO avoids the single-mode collapse exhibited by GRPO and closely recovers the target mode allocation. Applied to text-to-image prompt adaptation, DARS-GRPO consistently improves image and prompt diversity across datasets, Policy LMs, and reward settings while maintaining good semantic alignment. These results show that density-aware reward scaling provides a lightweight way to improve coverage of diverse high-reward outcomes within existing reinforcement-learning pipelines. National University of Singapore 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning is typically formulated to maximize expected return, which can drive outcome-level probability mass toward a small subset of high-reward outcomes ( GX-Chen et al. 2025 ) . While desirable for conventional control problems, this behavior is limiting in domains where multiple distinct outcomes are simultaneously valuable. In generative modeling, scientific discovery, and structured prediction, the objective is often not merely to identify a high-reward solution, but to learn a policy that maintains broad coverage over the high-reward outcome space. Several approaches have been proposed to promote such diversity. Entropy-regularized RL encourages stochastic action selection, but action-level stochasticity does not in general specify a desired distribution over terminal outcomes ( Haarnoja et al. 2018 ) . Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) instead target reward-proportional sampling, providing a principled framework for generating diverse high-reward samples ( Bengio et al. 2023 ) . Applying GFlowNet-style objectives to autoregressive pretrained models generally requires formulating generation through flow- or trajectory-based objectives rather than retaining an unchanged policy-gradient training pipeline ( Yun et al. 2025 ) . Inverse Probability Scaling (IPS) offers another route by inversely scaling reward according to terminal-outcome visitation probability ( Sinha et al. 2026 ) . In continuous or high-dimensional outcome spaces, however, exact repeated outcomes may be rare or may not provide a meaningful notion of semantic equivalence. We introduce Density-Aware Reward Scaling (DARS), a simple framework for encouraging a policy that has reward-proportional behavior within standard policy-gradient reinforcement learning. DARS is motivated by the limitations of IPS and replaces discrete visitation frequency with an estimate of local outcome density in continuous outcome spaces. For each on-policy rollout group, outcomes that lie in densely populated regions receive proportionally reduced rewards, while high-reward outcomes in underrepresented regions receive greater relative rewards. This density scaling is applied before advantage estimation and requires no modification to the underlying policy-gradient objective. Importantly, DARS introduces no learned density model, critic, auxiliary loss, or specialized policy architecture; instead it simply modifies reward processing within the existing RL pipeline. Our central contribution is a simple mechanism for mitigating outcome collapse and promoting coverage of diverse, high-reward regions within standard policy-gradient training. We validate DARS through controlled synthetic experiments that establish its ability to approximate reward-proportional sampling, followed by text-to-image prompt adaptation experiments demonstrating improved diversity while preserving generation quality, and kernel-width ablations that provide mechanistic evidence for its density-aware reward scaling. 2 Related Work Mode collapse in RL and loss of diversity: Mode collapse is widely associated with generative models that represent only a small subset of a multimodal data distribution. An analogous failure occurs in reinforcement learning at the level of terminal outcomes: even when multiple trajectories or solutions receive similar rewards, expected-return optimization concentrates the learned policy on a narrow subset of them, reducing the diversity of generated solutions in language and image generation ( Kirk et al. 2024 ; Chen et al. 2026 ) . Existing approaches mitigate this behavior through entropy regularization, KL constraints, reward shaping, or diversity-aware objectives ( Schulman et al. 2017 ; Liu et al. 2026 ) , yet they do not directly control the distribution of terminal outcomes. Recent work instead attributes outcome collapse to expected-return optimization itself, where an outcome’s aggregate learning signal is amplified by its current sampling probability, creating a rich-get-richer feedback loop ( Sinha et al. 2026 ) . Reward-proportional methods address this issue by sampling outcomes in proportion to their rewards: GFlowNets achieve this through specialized flow-conservation objectives and have been extended to multi-objective optimization, continuous state spaces, prompt adaptation, and language-model reasoning ( Bengio et al. 2021 ; Bengio et al. 2023 ; Jain et al. 2023 ; Lahlou et al. 2023 ; Zhu et al. 2026 ) , while IPS instead rescales rewards using inverse visitation probabilities estimated from empirical outcome frequencies ( Sinha et al. 2026 ) . However, empirical visitation frequencies become ineffective in continuous outcome spaces, where exact outcome repetitions are exceedingly rare. Concurrent work ( Chen et al. 2026 ) , also adjusts GRPO rewards using within-group semantic redundancy for mathematical reasoning in LLMs. In contrast, we study density-aware reward scaling as a mechanism for reward-proportional sampling in continuous outcome spaces and directly evaluate recovery of the target reward distribution. Prompt Adaptation and Image Generation: Loss of output diversity has become increasingly visible in reinforcement learning from human feedback and other forms of large-language-model post-training ( Ouyang et al. 2022 ; Kirk et al. 2024 ; Chen et al. 2026 ) . Reward optimization can favor a narrow set of response styles or semantic patterns even when many responses are valid. In practice, this behavior is often moderated with KL regularization, reward mixing, early stopping, or stochastic decoding. Prompt-optimization methods learn rewrites that improve text-to-image quality or alignment ( Hao et al. 2023 ) , while PAG learns diverse effective prompts with a GFlowNet formulation over prompt-generation trajectories ( Yun et al. 2025 ) . CADS acts at diffusion inference time by annealing the conditioning signal during sampling. 3 Density-Aware Reward Scaling (DARS) IPS shows that reward-proportional sampling can be achieved by inversely scaling rewards according to outcome probabilities under the current policy ( Sinha et al. 2026 ) , but estimating these probabilities through exact visitation frequencies does not extend naturally to continuous outcome spaces, where repeated outcomes are unlikely. DARS instead represents outcomes in a continuous feature space where distances capture meaningful similarity between outcomes. This representation allows visitation to be defined over local regions rather than exact outcome identities. DARS estimates the local density of each sampled outcome within its on-policy rollout group and inversely scales its reward by this density, reducing reinforcement of densely sampled regions while relatively favoring underrepresented high-reward regions. 3.1 Density Let 𝒪 \mathcal{O} denote the outcome space and let ϕ : 𝒪 → ℝ n \phi:\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n} be a representation map that embeds outcomes into a feature space. For an outcome o i ∈ 𝒪 o_{i}\in\mathcal{O} , let y i = ϕ ⁡ ( o i ) ∈ ℝ n y_{i}=\phi(o_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{n} denote its representation. Given an on-policy rollout group containing G G such y i y_{i} and their corresponding rewards R i ≥ 0 R_{i}\geq 0 , DARS computes the relative local density of each outcome only with respect to the outcomes in the same rollout group. For a nonnegative kernel K h K_{h} , this estimate is ρ i = ∑ j = 1 G K h ​ ( y i , y j ) , \rho_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{G}K_{h}(y_{i},y_{j}), (1) where h h controls how strongly nearby outcomes contribute to the local density. One choice is the Gaussian kernel, K h ​ ( y i , y j ) = exp ⁡ ( − ∥ y i − y j ∥ 2 2 2 ​ h 2 ) , K_{h}(y_{i},y_{j})=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert y_{i}-y_{j}\rVert_{2}^{2}}{2h^{2}}\right), (2) which assigns greater weight to nearby outcomes and smoothly decreases the contribution of outcomes as their distance increases. GRPO uses a clipped policy-ratio objective, and estimates advantages from groups of sampled outputs ( Shao et al. 2024 ) . It replaces each task reward R i R_{i} with the density-scaled reward R ~ i \widetilde{R}_{i} from Equation ( 3 ), after which the group-relative advantage is computed as A i = R ~ i − R ~ ¯ s R ~ , A_{i}=\frac{\widetilde{R}_{i}-\overline{\widetilde{R}}}{s_{\widetilde{R}}}, (4) where R ~ ¯ \overline{\widetilde{R}} and s R ~ s_{\widetilde{R}} are the within-group mean and standard deviation of the scaled rewards. The resulting advantages are passed to the standard GRPO objective without further modification. For each conditioning input, DARS-GRPO samples an on-policy rollout group and evaluates its task rewards. It then computes the within-group local-density scores, scales and normalizes the rewards to obtain group-relative advantages, and applies the standard GRPO policy update without further modification. Thus, DARS requires no change to the GRPO policy ratio, clipped surrogate objective, policy architecture, or optimization procedure; its sole intervention is density-aware reward scaling before advantage normalization. 3.3 Behavior At either kernel width extremes, as h → 0 h\to 0 , ρ i ≈ 1 \rho_{i}\approx 1 and the rewards remain unchanged; as h → ∞ h\to\infty , ρ i ≈ G \rho_{i}\approx G and group-relative advantage normalization cancels the shared reward scale. The primary comparison is against GRPO: both methods use the same policy, environment, and terminal reward, but only DARS corrects for local outcome collapse. GFlowNet provides a reward-proportional reference with a different training objective. The experiment is a controlled empirical test of whether DARS approaches the normalized reward distribution. We use complementary metrics because no single score captures all forms of distributional mismatch in a multimodal setting. Mean raw reward is estimated as the empirical average of r ⁡ ( x ) r(x) over sampled terminal states. Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) and histogram total variation (Hist. TV) compare the empirical and target densities on a 100 × 100 100\times 100 grid. Sliced Wasserstein-2 ( SW 2 \mathrm{SW}_{2} ) ( Kolouri et al. 2019 ) , energy distance ( Székely et al. 2013 ) , and Sinkhorn divergence ( Feydy et al. 2019 ) compare generated and target samples directly and measure geometric mismatch. RBF maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) ( Gretton et al. 2012 ) is reported at several bandwidths: small bandwidths emphasize local component shape, whereas large bandwidths emphasize mode allocation and global structure. Sliced Wasserstein-2 and energy distance use ten repetitions of 20,000 20{,}000 samples, while Sinkhorn divergence uses 500 500 samples. For mode-level evaluation, each terminal state is assigned to its nearest target center. From these assignments, we compute the mass of each mode, the minimum mode mass, and mode TV which measures deviation from uniform target mode weights. Precision is the fraction of generated samples lying inside k k -nearest-neighbor neighborhoods of target samples, while recall is the fraction of target samples covered by neighborhoods induced by generated samples ( Kynkäänniemi et al. 2019 ) . Precision therefore measures off-target generation, whereas recall diagnoses missing support and mode collapse. We measure Wasserstein error at two scales: the between-mode term evaluates mode weights and centers, while the within-mode term evaluates each mode’s mean and covariance. Their sum defines the hierarchical score, W hier = W between + W within . W_{\mathrm{hier}}=W_{\mathrm{between}}+W_{\mathrm{within}}. Since the target assigns approximately 0.05 probability mass outside this region, we report the calibration error | m outside − 0.05 | |m_{\mathrm{outside}}-0.05| , for which lower values indicate better agreement with the target. 4.2 Results and Interpretation The primary result is the comparison with GRPO. In the reported run, GRPO concentrates on a single high-reward mode, whereas DARS-GRPO assigns substantial mass to all four modes and approaches their target weights. The DARS-GRPO point estimates are closer to the target than GRPO across the metrics reported in Table 1 . GRPO’s higher mean raw reward reflects tight concentration near one of four equally high peaks, rather than agreement with the normalized reward distribution. Thus, within this controlled environment, the reported run provides evidence that density reweighting prevents the evaluated policy from concentrating on one mode, recovers the correct mode weights, and improves global geometric agreement with the known target relative to GRPO. This is the central controlled contribution of the experiment. DARS-GRPO closely matches, and on several key metrics surpasses, GFlowNet despite requiring only a simple reward-scaling modification within a standard policy-gradient pipeline. Both methods achieve identical precision, indicating equally accurate recovery of high-reward outcomes. DARS consistently improves metrics that capture the global reward distribution, including sliced Wasserstein, energy distance, mode total variation, minimum mode mass, hierarchical Wasserstein error, HDR outside mass, and most larger-bandwidth MMD and Sinkhorn metrics, demonstrating more faithful recovery of target mode proportions and global geometry. GFlowNet performs slightly better on metrics emphasizing fine-scale local density, such as Jensen–Shannon divergence, histogram total variation, within-mode Wasserstein error, recall, and small-bandwidth MMD, reflecting its specialized flow-based objective. Nevertheless, these results show that a lightweight modification to conventional policy-gradient RL is sufficient to achieve reward-proportional behavior that is competitive with a substantially more sophisticated algorithmic framework. Having established in a controlled setting that DARS approximates reward-proportional sampling, we next ask whether this property is useful in a real continuous-output RL problem where the target reward distribution is unknown. 5 Text-to-Image Prompt Adaptation Figure 2: Overview of DARS-GRPO for text-to-image prompt adaptation. GRPO then uses these scaled rewards to update only the prompt-rewriting policy. 5.1 Motivation Prompt adaptation for image generation refers to the setting in which a language model rewrites the input prompt to match a desired set of outcomes before image generation. Text-to-image prompt adaptation provides a natural real-world benchmark for evaluating reward-proportional reinforcement learning. Unlike the synthetic experiments in Section 4 , where the target reward distribution is explicitly known, the reward-proportional distribution over generated images is intractable and cannot be directly characterized. A single text prompt typically admits many semantically faithful realizations that differ in composition, viewpoint, lighting, object arrangement, or artistic style while remaining equally valid. Since the underlying reward distribution is unavailable, directly measuring reward-proportional sampling is infeasible. Instead, we evaluate its consequences through observable proxies. If DARS successfully distributes probability mass across multiple high-reward regions, it should produce a more diverse set of images while preserving prompt alignment and image quality. We therefore measure visual diversity together with alignment and preference metrics as an indirect estimate of improved coverage of the latent reward landscape. Consequently, the objective is not merely to identify a single high-reward image, but to maintain coverage over the diverse set of high-quality outcomes consistent with the prompt. Since input prompts are the conditioning signal in diffusion models, semantically faithful prompt rewrites help steer the generation in desired directions. Learning a distribution over such rewrites therefore provides an effective mechanism for exploring multiple high-reward image modes while keeping the underlying image generator fixed. Following this formulation, we fine-tune a language model using reinforcement learning to rewrite input prompts. Images generated from the rewritten prompts are rewarded as defined in section 5.2 . Since multiple visually distinct images can achieve comparable rewards, broader coverage of the latent reward landscape should translate to greater image diversity without sacrificing fidelity. To quantify this diversity, we measure distances in the DINOv2 representation space as a proxy for perceptual similarity ( Oquab et al. 2023 ) . Image diversity is measured in DINOv2 CLS representation space using the Vendi Score ( Friedman and Dieng 2023 ) of the cosine-similarity matrix of L2-normalized CLS embeddings, and the mean pairwise Euclidean distance between CLS embeddings. Diversity metrics are computed within each group of rewrites or images generated for the same original prompt and then averaged across the evaluation set, following within-prompt conditional evaluation. For the experiments in Section 5 , we demonstrate the direct effects of varying kernel widths on image-diversity produced by DARS (Table 3 ). Diversity metrics consistently peak at intermediate kernel widths and degrade when the bandwidth is either too small or too large, while image quality remains largely unchanged. This behavior reflects how DARS estimates local outcome density. With a very small kernel width, nearly every generated image appears isolated, causing density estimates to be dominated by self-similarity and resulting in almost uniform reward scaling. Conversely, an excessively large kernel width treats distant images as belonging to the same neighborhood, oversmoothing density estimates and diminishing the relative reward differences that encourage exploration. Intermediate kernel widths instead resolve meaningful local neighborhoods allowing for effective density estimation in DARS. 7 Limitations DARS relies on a meaningful representation space and kernel bandwidth for estimating local outcome density. Its effectiveness may therefore degrade when embedding distances poorly reflect semantic similarity or when no single bandwidth captures the relevant neighborhood structure. The pairwise density computation also scales quadratically with rollout-group size, potentially limiting its use with large groups. Our experiments focus on a controlled navigation task and text-to-image prompt adaptation with fixed image representations and generators. Broader evaluation across RL domains, policy architectures, and learned representations is needed. Finally, our results establish empirical approximation to reward-proportional sampling rather than a general convergence guarantee. 8 Conclusion We introduced Density-Aware Reward Scaling (DARS), a lightweight mechanism for promoting diverse, high-reward outcomes within standard policy-gradient training. By inversely scaling rewards using local outcome density, DARS counteracts repeated reinforcement of densely sampled regions without requiring a critic, auxiliary objective, learned density model, or modified policy-gradient loss. In a controlled multimodal navigation task, DARS-GRPO prevents the mode collapse observed with GRPO and closely recovers target mode allocation. In text-to-image prompt adaptation, it consistently increases prompt and image diversity across datasets, Policy LMs, and reward settings while retaining semantic fidelity. These results position density-aware reward scaling as a simple yet effective approach to improving outcome coverage. References Bengio et al. (2021) E. Bengio, M. Jain, M. Korablyov, D.
